title: Klein v. PepsiCo, Inc.
lead: An aircraft seller’s withdrawal comes after enough conduct to form a contract, but comparable jets and compensable losses defeat forced delivery of this particular plane.

actors.name: Eugene Klein
actors.role: Prospective purchaser seeking a used Gulfstream G-II.

actors.name: Universal Jet Sales and Patrick Janas
PepsiCo
actors.role: Owner and proposed seller of the aircraft.

actors.name: Rashid, Welsch, and Donald Kendall
actors.role: PepsiCo vice president, sales broker, and chairman involved at distinct stages.

proceedings: The district court found a $4.6 million PepsiCo–UJS contract and ordered specific performance.
The Fourth Circuit affirmed formation findings but reversed the equitable remedy.
The case returned for a damages trial.
limits: The related UJS purchase and Klein resale are distinct contracts with distinct prices and deposits. No damages amount or entitlement to a particular resale profit was determined.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Klein uses an aircraft reseller to negotiate for PepsiCo’s jet
sections.cue: Who offered to buy from whom?
paragraphs: Eugene Klein wanted a used Gulfstream G-II corporate jet and engaged Universal Jet Sales, or UJS. Its president Patrick Janas located PepsiCo’s aircraft. UJS planned to buy it and resell it to Klein, making two related transactions rather than a single direct purchase.

Klein’s pilot and mechanic inspected the plane in New York, and Klein inspected it in Arkansas on March 29, 1986, with Janas and PepsiCo vice president Rashid present. Klein gave Janas $200,000 and authorized a $4.4 million offer. Janas transmitted it by telex March 31 to PepsiCo’s broker, Welsch, referring to satisfactory factory inspection and a definitive contract.

PepsiCo countered at $4.7 million. The parties reached $4.6 million, which Janas accepted by telex April 3. His confirmation referred to a $100,000 down payment and requested the corporate seller’s proper name. UJS intended a $4.75 million resale to Klein. The different sums belonged to those separate relationships and negotiating stages.

sources.pinpoint: Proposed aircraft sale; assigned p.109; 845 F.2d at 78

sections.title: The parties prepare closing documents and undertake the agreed inspection
sections.cue: What remained wrong with the aircraft?
paragraphs: Janas circulated agreements for both sales and sent PepsiCo a bill of sale. PepsiCo executed it and placed it with the escrow agent. Its lawyer said the proposed agreement was acceptable except for the delivery date. PepsiCo received the required $100,000 down payment without objecting to the confirming telex.

The plane went to Savannah April 7 for inspection attended by the buyer’s mechanic and PepsiCo’s maintenance representative. Most problems were resolved, but cosmetic work and cracked turbine blades remained. Examination disclosed eight to eleven cracks in right-engine blades, with estimated repairs of $25,000 to $28,000. The trial court later found that PepsiCo agreed to pay for those repairs.

sources.pinpoint: Proposed sale; Formation evidence; assigned pp.109–111

sections.title: PepsiCo’s chairman decides to keep the jet as closing approaches
sections.cue: How did the parties respond to withdrawal?
paragraphs: The aircraft returned to New York April 9. Despite Rashid’s desire to ground it, it flew that evening to collect PepsiCo chairman Donald Kendall from Dulles. On April 10 Kendall asked Rashid to remove it from the market.

Janas learned of the withdrawal and told Klein on April 11, the scheduled closing date, that PepsiCo would not tender. Klein demanded delivery from UJS April 14; UJS demanded it from PepsiCo and expressed satisfaction with the inspection. PepsiCo replied that no agreement had resulted and that Klein had not been ready to proceed. Kendall’s desire to retain the aircraft explained the withdrawal but did not decide whether the earlier conduct had already bound PepsiCo.

sections.title: The trial court finds a contract and requires transfer
sections.cue: Why did the appellate court sustain formation?
paragraphs: After extensive findings, the district court concluded that UJS and PepsiCo had contracted for the $4.6 million sale and ordered specific performance. On appeal PepsiCo argued that no obligation could arise before it signed the final sales agreement.

Judge Ervin’s Fourth Circuit opinion reviewed findings for clear error, giving particular weight to credibility determinations supported by corroborating evidence. The April 3 telex, payment, absence of objection, counsel’s acceptance of the memorializing document, deposited bill of sale, inspection, and admissions of offer acceptance supported a completed bargain. The later writing could be a memorial rather than a condition of formation. Mere disagreement with that reading did not produce a firm conviction of mistake.

The result was record-specific. Parties can condition formation on a signed document or withdraw while negotiations remain incomplete; PepsiCo failed to show clear error in finding these negotiations had already produced an agreement.

sources.pinpoint: Procedure and formation; assigned pp.110–111; 845 F.2d at 79

sections.title: The supported repair promise answers the inspection objection
sections.cue: Which ancillary arguments did the panel resolve only by reference?
paragraphs: PepsiCo separately argued that inspection remained unsatisfactory because the buyers would not accept the plane in its existing condition. The district court found that PepsiCo’s agreement to repair satisfied the condition and alternatively that refusal to tender excused it. The appellate court relied on the supported repair finding, without needing a general ruling about prevention or excuse.

A footnote also affirmed rejection of PepsiCo’s arguments about the statute of frauds, Klein’s intended-beneficiary status, and alleged rescission of the Klein–UJS agreement on the district court’s reasoning. The panel did not independently elaborate new tests for those issues.

sources.pinpoint: Inspection condition and sole footnote; assigned pp.111–112 n.1

sections.title: Available replacement jets make monetary relief adequate
sections.cue: Why did the specific-performance order fail despite a valid contract?
paragraphs: Virginia’s Uniform Commercial Code § 2-716 permitted specific performance for unique goods or other proper circumstances, but retained the principle that an adequate damages remedy ordinarily made compelled performance inappropriate. The district court called the jet unique and relied on supposed inability to cover. Reviewing the remedy for abuse of discretion, the Fourth Circuit found neither ground supported.

Klein’s expert identified twenty-one G-IIs on the market, including three roughly comparable planes. His chief pilot acknowledged alternatives. UJS obtained two G-IIs and offered them to Klein after the failed transaction, and Klein bid on two others himself. Individual aircraft differences did not show that a suitable replacement was unavailable.

Klein said rising G-II prices led him to choose a G-III instead. Greater replacement expense could be compensated in damages. The trial judge repeatedly said damages would make him whole, and Klein had described a resale-for-profit objective. On this record money could address the loss without compelling PepsiCo to deliver this plane.

sources.pinpoint: Specific performance; assigned pp.111–112; 845 F.2d at 80

sections.title: Formation stands while remedy returns for a damages trial
sections.cue: What did the partial reversal leave unresolved?
paragraphs: On April 25, 1988, the Fourth Circuit affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded for trial on damages. Judges Sprouse and Chief District Judge Britt joined Ervin without a separate opinion. The contract finding remained, but the order transferring the aircraft did not.

The decision did not excuse PepsiCo’s breach, set a monetary award, or guarantee Klein his anticipated resale margin. It separates formation from remedy: losing a no-contract argument does not automatically make forced delivery appropriate, and distinctiveness or higher replacement cost does not alone establish inadequacy of damages.

sources.pinpoint: Judgment; Court and decision; assigned pp.108–112
